# Expert Question 1 — Part I signal-strength definition and turbulence model scope

## Problem Understanding

Problem 2018_A (HF ocean reflection). Part I asks: for a 100-W HF constant carrier
from a point source on land, below the MUF, determine the strength of the FIRST
ocean reflection (after one ionospheric reflection) on a turbulent ocean, compare
it with the calm-ocean first reflection, then count the maximum number of further
calm-ocean hops before SNR falls below a 10 dB threshold. Parts II–IV extend the
same model to rugged vs smooth terrain and to a moving shipboard receiver.

## Modeling Objective and Stage

Formulating the per-hop path-loss/reflection model. Everything downstream
(calm vs turbulent comparison, hop count, terrain, ship) hangs on the geometry
and power definition chosen here.

## Unresolved Strategic Decision

What exactly should "strength of the first reflection" mean, and how should
turbulence enter the model? Three candidates:

**A. Fixed nominal geometry, received power at a specified receiving point.**
Assume a representative 1- or 2-hop circuit (e.g. ~150–500 km, one F2
ionospheric hop + one ocean reflection), free-space spread from the point
source, ionospheric absorption, and a Fresnel reflection coefficient at the
ocean surface. Turbulence enters as: (i) a reduced effective surface
reflectivity (wave-roughness scattering modeled with an rms-height
slope model) and (ii) a small extra spread/loss term. "Strength" = received
power (dBW or dBm) at the receiving point for turbulent vs calm.

**B. Field strength at the ocean surface / reflection coefficient ratio only.**
"Strength of the first reflection" = |r_turbulent / r_calm| as a dB ratio of
the reflected wave, independent of propagation distance. The hop count then
uses only the per-reflection dB loss.

**C. Full stochastic sea-state model.**
Full JONSWAP sea spectrum, random surface realization, Monte Carlo over wave
phases for the reflected field. Physically richest, but expensive and less
reproducible, with parameters (significant wave height, spectrum) not pinned by
the provided data.

My recommendation is A: it gives a concrete comparable power level (which is
what "strength" and the later SNR/hop-count questions need), keeps turbulence
parameterized by rms wave height and slope (a small, defensible extension of
the calm Fresnel coefficient), and stays reproducible. B is too weak to support
the SNR hop count without an arbitrary reference; C is overkill for a short-note
deliverable and under-pinned by data.

## Why It Matters

The choice fixes the meaning of every Part I number and the units of the
turbulence attenuation, and Parts II–IV reuse this same per-hop loss chain.

# Expert Question 2 — SNR floor (receiver noise) for the 10 dB hop-count threshold

## Problem Understanding

Part I, per the settled framework (received power at a defined receiving
point, turbulence as a reduced effective ocean reflectivity plus a small
scattering loss term), asks for the maximum number of calm-ocean hops before
the signal falls below a usable SNR threshold of 10 dB.

## Modeling Objective and Stage

Per-hop loss chain is settled: free-space spread from a 100 W point source,
F2 ionospheric hop (small vertical-incidence absorption at ~10–15 MHz, order
tenths of dB per ITU-R P.531 practice, with f ≈ 0.85 × MUF), ocean-surface
Fresnel reflection (calm: |r| ≈ 1 at grazing; turbulent: |r| reduced by rms
wave-height/slope roughness), and a receiver antenna gain. What is NOT settled
is the noise floor against which the 10 dB threshold is measured.

## Unresolved Strategic Decision

How to define the receiver noise floor N for SNR = S/N ≥ 10 dB. Candidates:

**A. Thermal noise with an assumed narrowband channel.**
N = kTB with a specified channel bandwidth (e.g. B = 3 kHz SSB, the standard
HF voice channel) and system noise figure (e.g. NF = 5 dB over 290 K).
Everything then follows from the settled per-hop chain plus one documented
receiver assumption.

**B. Matched to a stated receiver sensitivity.**
Take a typical HF receiver sensitivity (e.g. −110 dBm in 3 kHz) as the 10-dB
SNR point and back out the effective noise floor. Ties the model to a device
spec that is not in the provided data.

**C. Treat the 10 dB threshold as a pure path-loss budget.**
Ignore thermal noise and ask for received power to stay 10 dB above an
implicit −∞ floor; the hop count is then just total loss ≤ (P_tx − 10 dB −
some fixed reference). This is circular without a reference and would just
reintroduce the arbitrary reference B was rejected for.

My recommendation is A: B = 3 kHz (SSB voice, the stated use case — weather
and traffic reports) with a 5 dB system noise figure. It is the standard,
defensible HF receiver assumption, makes the hop count a concrete integer, and
its sensitivity can be shown in one extra line (B = 1 kHz CW-style vs 3 kHz).

## Why It Matters

The hop count — the headline integer of Part I — is the difference between the
total per-hop loss chain and the noise floor. Different floors shift that
integer by ±1, so the floor definition must be pinned before computing.

# Expert Question 3 — Modeling the ship's motion (Part III)

## Problem Understanding

Parts I–II are settled: received-power per-hop loss chain (free-space spread,
ionospheric hop, ocean Fresnel reflection with turbulent reflectivity reduced
by rms wave height/slope plus a small scattering loss term) and the 10 dB SNR
threshold measured against thermal noise kTB with B = 3 kHz, NF = 5 dB, 290 K,
with a sensitivity line on B. Part III asks how the model changes for a ship
moving on a turbulent ocean, and how long it can remain in communication using
the same multi-hop path.

## Modeling Objective and Stage

The ship adds: (i) motion relative to a fixed multi-hop path, and (ii) a
moving, rough receive surface (the ship rides the waves, antenna height
oscillates). Both are second-order on the per-hop loss chain relative to the
first-hop numbers.

## Unresolved Strategic Decision

How to represent the ship's motion when computing "how long the ship remains in
communication." Candidates:

**A. Geometric path-length drift only.**
Fix the multi-hop path (fixed transmitter, fixed number of hops, fixed hop
lengths); the ship moves at speed v (assume 15 knots). At each time step,
recompute the receiver-to-last-hop-endpoint distance and the resulting
free-space loss and grazing angle; communication ends when SNR < 10 dB.
Ship-borne antenna height oscillation is folded into an averaged effective
height (mean draft + significant-wave-height correction) rather than
simulated instant by instant.

**B. Full Doppler / time-varying channel.**
Add Doppler spread from both ship motion and wave motion (Brillouin/Bragg
scattering at the Bragg wavenumber), model the channel as time-varying with a
fading rate, and ask for coherence time or a fade-budget lifetime. Physically
richer, but the "how long in communication" answer then depends on a fading
threshold that the problem does not state.

**C. Ship-as-point-moving-on-average-surface.**
Treat the ship exactly as the land receiver except at a time-varying position,
ignoring antenna height modulation and Doppler entirely. Simplest; likely
understates the effect of riding waves on the local reflection geometry.

My recommendation is A: it keeps the answer a concrete time in hours, reuses
the settled per-hop chain unchanged, and the height-averaging is a documented
one-line assumption. B's coherence-time answer is not what "how long in
communication using the same path" asks; C drops the very effect (moving on a
turbulent ocean) the question is about.

## Why It Matters

Fixes the Part III deliverable (a time, in hours) and states precisely what
"same multi-hop path" means as the ship moves.
expert_answers:
**A is the correct choice.** "Strength of the first reflection" must be a received power at a defined receiving point, because Part I's SNR threshold and hop count require an absolute power level in dBW/dBm, not a dimensionless ratio. Only A yields that.

Turbulence should enter as a multiplicative reduction of the ocean's effective Fresnel reflectivity, parameterized by rms wave height and surface slope, plus a small diffuse-scattering loss term. This keeps the calm case as the baseline Fresnel coefficient and makes the turbulent-vs-calm comparison a clean dB difference.

B cannot support the SNR hop count without an arbitrary reference power, and C is under-pinned by the provided data and unnecessary for a short-note deliverable. A is also the only option that transfers cleanly to Parts II–IV, where terrain roughness and ship motion modify the same per-hop loss chain.

**A is the correct choice.** The 10 dB SNR threshold is meaningless without an explicit noise floor, and thermal noise with a documented narrowband channel is the only option that yields a concrete, reproducible integer hop count.

Use N = kTB with B = 3 kHz (SSB voice — matching the stated weather/traffic-report use case) and a system noise figure of 5 dB over 290 K. This is the standard HF receiver assumption, requires only one documented parameter, and keeps the hop count a clean integer.

B ties the model to an unspecified device spec not present in the provided data, and C is circular — it merely reintroduces the arbitrary reference already rejected in Exchange 1.

One refinement: report the hop count's sensitivity to B (e.g. 1 kHz CW vs 3 kHz SSB), since the floor shifts the integer by ±1. That single extra line preserves reproducibility without widening the model.

**A is the correct choice.** "How long the ship remains in communication using the same multi-hop path" asks for a duration in hours, which only a geometric path-length drift model yields directly. Fix the transmitter, hop count, and hop lengths; move the ship at v ≈ 15 knots; recompute receiver-to-last-hop-endpoint distance, free-space loss, and grazing angle each step; declare loss of communication when SNR < 10 dB. Fold antenna-height oscillation into an averaged effective height (mean draft plus significant-wave-height correction) as a stated one-line assumption.

B answers a different question — coherence time under fading — and its lifetime depends on an unstated fade threshold. C discards the moving-on-a-turbulent-ocean effect the question is specifically about. A reuses the settled per-hop chain unchanged and keeps the deliverable concrete and reproducible.
